name: Benjamin Franklin effect
statement: Doing someone a favour is said to raise your liking for them, so asking a rival for a small favour wins him over faster than granting him one.
meaning: The claim runs backwards from the obvious one. Ordinary reciprocity says the person who receives a kindness warms to the giver, and that idea has its own entry here. This one says the giver warms to the receiver. The person who changes is the one who did the work, and what changes is the rating of the person the work was done for. The usual explanation borrows from cognitive dissonance, which also has its own entry: helping someone you dislike is hard to hold alongside disliking them, and the cheaper of the two thoughts to revise is the dislike. Effort justification makes a neighbouring claim about the thing effort buys rather than the person it was spent on.

origin.note: The name comes from an anecdote of the 1730s and the experiment is from 1969. Franklin was chosen clerk of the Pennsylvania General Assembly in 1736, and the year after a new member spoke at length against him. Franklin heard the man owned a scarce book, asked to borrow it, returned it in about a week with a warm note, and reports that the two became friends. He wrote this down in 1788, at home, in the third part of the autobiography. Who first attached his name to the laboratory effect was not traced in this search.

evidence: The 1969 paper is the whole of the experimental basis, and it could not be read for this entry. Crossref records it as Jecker and Landy, "Liking a Person as a Function of Doing Him a Favour", Human Relations 22(4), 371-378, dated August 1969. What stopped this session was not a paywall. On 21 September 2026 the SAGE article page answered every request with a Cloudflare bot challenge, under a plain and a browser-like user agent alike, so no subscription page was ever reached. Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all record the article as closed with no repository copy, and Semantic Scholar notes the abstract as withheld by the publisher. So this page carries no sample size, no condition means and no effect size from it. Two scholarly descriptions of the study were obtained instead. Orehek's chapter says participants who performed a favour for someone they had previously seen negatively or neutrally came to like that person more. Nguyen and Nguyen say participants asked by the experimenter himself to return prize money liked him more than those asked through an intermediary or not asked at all. Both sentences are the citing authors' summaries rather than Jecker and Landy's wording, and neither could be checked against the paper. The fuller account that circulates, which adds a student count and a quiz contest, was found only in encyclopedia entries and popular essays, none of them citing a page. It is not repeated here as fact. What can be read is Franklin. He asked for the loan of "a certain very scarce and curious book", the member "sent it immediately", and at the next sitting he spoke to Franklin "(which he had never done before), and with great civility". Franklin presents the episode as "another instance of the truth of an old maxim I had learned", and quotes the maxim: "He that has once done you a kindness will be more ready to do you another, than he whom you yourself have obliged."

examples.text: A neighbour you have never warmed to asks to borrow your ladder, and you lend it. The claim is about what happens in you rather than in him. Having gone out of your way for someone you do not much like is easier to settle by liking him more.

Asked to take a shift for a colleague she finds tiresome, a nurse agrees. A week later she describes him more warmly than before. Nothing he did changed in the meantime. The change is in the person who did the favour.

A senior engineer spends an afternoon on a junior's problem and hears nothing back. Reciprocity predicts the junior warming to him. This effect predicts the other leg: the engineer ends up thinking better of the junior he helped.

replication.headline: No repeat of the 1969 experiment was found. One later experiment tested the same claim by a different route and supported it.
replication.detail: Semantic Scholar's citation graph listed 66 works citing Jecker and Landy on 21 September 2026, and every title in that list was read. None is a replication of their procedure. Most of the citing work is on help-seeking, volunteering, negotiation, job design and social engineering, and it treats the 1969 result as a premise. Neither author published a repeat: Semantic Scholar's record for Jecker lists nothing after 1969. The nearest test is Niiya's 2016 experiment in The Journal of Social Psychology, built around the Japanese concept of amae rather than around Franklin. Its abstract reports that Japanese and American participants who were asked for help by a confederate liked the confederate more than a baseline, and that the confederate seemed more sociable and the relationship closer. Participants who helped without being asked showed no such rise. Only the abstract was obtained, so no sample size and no effect size from it appears here. The newest citing work, by Nguyen and Nguyen, is open and was read in full. It interviews 30 people about small favours and never runs the 1969 procedure, so it adds no test of it. Schopler and Compere published an adjacent experiment in 1971 on how being kind or harsh to another changes liking for that person. The APA record refused this session as a robot, the text was not read, and nothing is claimed here about what it found.

limits: Both of the papers that matter are closed, and no refusal this session met was a paywall message. SAGE and Taylor and Francis each answered with a Cloudflare bot challenge, and the APA record for Schopler and Compere was blocked by Imperva. Unpaywall and OpenAlex record all three as closed with no repository copy, checked on 21 September 2026. That means the structured effect-size fields on this page are empty, and it means nobody writing about this effect from open sources is reading the experiment they are describing. The search covered Crossref, Europe PMC, PubMed, Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar including the full citation list of the 1969 paper, CiNii, the Internet Archive and web search, all on 21 September 2026. It found no direct replication, no meta-analysis and no preregistered test. Niiya's design differs from the 1969 one in the request, the requester and the outcome measures, so it tests the claim rather than the study. Franklin's own evidence is one episode from the 1730s, written down in 1788 by the man it flatters, and he never names the member or the book. The mechanism is also unsettled in a way this page cannot resolve: dissonance is the usual account, and the multilab failure of the induced-compliance paradigm recorded in entry 24 is a reason to hold that account loosely.
misreadings: Franklin is credited with the insight and did not claim it. He called it "an old maxim I had learned" and quoted it, which is a report of received folk wisdom rather than a discovery. Orehek's chapter shows how the slip travels: it introduces the maxim as something "offered by Ben Franklin, who stated" it. The story also grows in retelling. Franklin describes a new member who made a long speech against him in order to favour another candidate, not an enemy who hated him, and the favour asked was the loan of a book for a few days, returned in about a week with thanks. The lesson Franklin draws from it is about removing opposition rather than resenting it. Confusing the direction is the commonest error of all. Reciprocity, entry 120, is the claim that receiving a favour makes people well disposed to the giver, and it is a different and much better evidenced idea. Effort justification, entry 200, and the IKEA effect, entry 49, concern what effort does to the thing it produced, not to the person it was spent on. Finally, the name promises a documented bias. What sits behind it is one 1969 paper almost nobody has read, one 2016 experiment with a different design, and an anecdote.

sources.text: Franklin, B. The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, edited by Charles W. Eliot. Project Gutenberg ebook 148. The clerk of the Assembly passage and the maxim were read here in full.

Franklin, B. Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin, edited by Frank Woodworth Pine. Project Gutenberg ebook 20203. A second, independently edited text, used to confirm the passage word for word and for the editor's note dating the third part to August 1788.

Jecker, J., & Landy, D. (1969). Liking a Person as a Function of Doing Him a Favour. Human Relations, 22(4), 371-378. The experimental basis of the effect. Not read for this entry: the SAGE page answered with a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall, and Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar record no open copy. The bibliographic details come from Crossref.

Niiya, Y. (2016). Does a Favor Request Increase Liking Toward the Requester? The Journal of Social Psychology, 156(2), 211-221. The Taylor and Francis page answered with a Cloudflare bot challenge and no open copy is indexed, so the result quoted here is taken from the abstract at PubMed.

Schopler, J., & Compere, J. S. (1971). Effects of being kind or harsh to another on liking. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 20(2), 155-159. Listed because it exists; the APA record blocked this session as a robot, and the paper was not read for this entry.

Orehek, E. Goal Pursuit and Close Relationships: A People as Means Perspective. Chapter to appear in C. Kopetz & A. Fishbach (Eds.), The Motivation-Cognition Interface: From the Lab to the Real World. Cited for its one-line description of Jecker and Landy and for its attribution of the maxim to Franklin himself.

Nguyen, Q. A., & Nguyen, H. P. (2025). The Franklin effect in social and workplace contexts: A qualitative study on how small requests foster interpersonal bonding. Ho Chi Minh City Open University Journal of Science - Economics and Business Administration, 16(9). Open, and read in full. An interview study, not a test of the 1969 design, and cited here for its second-hand description of that design.
